questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Inverse of a 2x2 Matrix
questions.worked_solution:
Given a $2\times 2$ matrix

$$
Z=[\begin{aligned}a & b \\ c & d\end{aligned}],
$$

the inverse of $Z$ can be found using the following formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Z}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{det(Z)}[\begin{aligned}d & -b \\ -c & a\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

First, we compute the determinant:

$$
det(Z)=1\cdot 8-3\cdot 2=2
$$

Using the formula, then, the inverse is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{Z}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{det(Z)}[\begin{aligned}d & -b \\ -c & a\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}8 & -2 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

We can verify the result as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Z{Z}^{-1} & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 8\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}8 & -2 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & ={I}_{2}\,✓ \\ {Z}^{-1}Z & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}8 & -2 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & ={I}_{2}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

First, we compute the determinant:

$$
det(C)=3\cdot 0-1\cdot 3=-3
$$

Using the formula, then, the inverse is given by

Given a $2\times 2$ matrix

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}a & b \\ c & d\end{aligned}],
$$

the inverse of $B$ can be found using the following formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}{B}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{det(B)}[\begin{aligned}d & -b \\ -c & a\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

First, we compute the determinant:

$$
det(B)=2\cdot 0-1\cdot 1=-1
$$

Using the formula, then, the inverse is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{B}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{det(B)}[\begin{aligned}d & -b \\ -c & a\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{(-1)}[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

We can verify the result as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}B{B}^{-1} & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & ={I}_{2}\,✓ \\ {B}^{-1}B & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & ={I}_{2}\,✓\end{aligned}

questions.problem:
Which of the matrices below are singular?

$$
H=[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}],\,J=[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 3 & 6\end{aligned}],\,K=[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 \\ 0 & 5 \\ -3 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
- For the matrix $H$, we have

$$
det(H)=5\cdot 0-3\cdot 0=0.
$$

Because $det(H)=0,$ we conclude that $H$ is not invertible. Since $H$ is a square matrix that is not invertible, we also say that $H$ is singular.

- For the matrix $J$, we have

$$
det(J)=2\cdot 6-3\cdot 4=0.
$$

Because $det(J)=0,$ we conclude that $J$ is not invertible. Since $J$ is a square matrix that is not invertible, we also say that $J$ is singular.

- The matrix $K$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix. So, it is not invertible. Since the matrix is not square, we can't say that it's singular.

Therefore, only $H$ and $J$ is singular.

questions.problem:
Which of the matrices below does **not** have an inverse?

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0\end{aligned}],\,B=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
- The matrix $A$ is a $1\times 2$ matrix. So, it is not invertible.

- For the matrix $B$, we have

$$
det(B)=0\cdot 0-(-1)\cdot 1=1.
$$

Because $det(B)\ne 0,$ we conclude that $B$ is invertible.

- For the matrix $C$, we have

$$
det(C)=1\cdot 2-2\cdot 1=0.
$$

Because $det(C)=0,$ we conclude that $C$ is not invertible.

Therefore, only $A$ and $C$ do not have an inverse.

$$

$$

Because $det(S)\ne 0,$ we conclude that $S$ is invertible.

$$

$$

Because $det(T)=0,$ we conclude that $T$ is not invertible. Since $T$ is a square matrix that is not invertible, we also say that $T$ is singular.

- For the matrix $U$, we have

$$
det(U)=0\cdot 0-1\cdot (-1)=1.
$$

Because $det(U)\ne 0,$ we conclude that $U$ is invertible.

Therefore, only $T$ is singular.

questions.problem: If $M=[\begin{aligned}t & 4 \\ t & 10\end{aligned}]$ is a singular matrix, calculate the value of $t.$
questions.worked_solution:
The matrix $M$ is singular if and only if $det(M)=0.$ Calculating the determinant, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}det(M) & =t\cdot 10-t\cdot 4 \\  & =10t-4t \\  & =6t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we set the determinant equal to $0$ and solve for $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}6t & =0 \\ t & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the value of $t$ is $t=0.$

is a singular matrix, calculate the value of $x.$

questions.problem: If $F=[\begin{aligned}3 & t \\ t & 3\end{aligned}]$ is a singular matrix, calculate the value(s) of $t.$
questions.worked_solution:
The matrix $F$ is singular if and only if $det(F)=0.$ Calculating the determinant, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}det(F) & =3\cdot 3-t\cdot t \\  & =9-{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we set the determinant equal to $0$ and solve for $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}9-{t}^{2} & =0 \\ {t}^{2} & =9 \\ t & =\pm 3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the values of $t$ are $t=\pm 3.$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{det(A)}[\begin{aligned}d & -b \\ -c & a\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

First, we compute the determinant:

$$
\det(A) = 1 \cdot 1 - 0 \cdot (-2) = 1
$$

Using the formula, then, the inverse is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{det(A)}[\begin{aligned}d & -b \\ -c & a\end{aligned}]. \\  & =\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}1 & -0 \\ -(-2) & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

We can verify the result as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A{A}^{-1} & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & ={I}_{2}\,✓ \\ {A}^{-1}A & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & ={I}_{2}\,✓\end{aligned}

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Solving for a Variable in a Singular Matrix
canonical_examples.problem:
If 
$[\begin{aligned}1-k & 2 \\ 2 & 1-k\end{aligned}]$
 is a singular matrix, calculate the value(s) of $k.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The matrix $A$ is singular if and only if $\det(A)=0.$ Calculating the determinant, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =(1-k)(1-k)-4 \\  & ={k}^{2}-2k-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we set the determinant equal to $0$ and solve for $k\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{k}^{2}-2k-3 & =0 \\ (k-3)(k+1) & =0 \\ k & =3,-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the values of $k$ are $k=3$ and $k=-1.$
